multiplechoiceresponse.p: A churn model is 97% accurate. Only 2% of accounts leave each month. What should you ask first?

choice.div: What does it add over the base rate, and how well does it rank the group we will act on?
Whether 97% is high enough to deploy.

div.p: With a 2% base rate, "nobody leaves" is 98% accurate. Accuracy alone says almost nothing about usefulness.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: The model ranks the whole base well but misses the high-value segment. What does that mean for the decision?

choice.div: Check performance on the segment you will act on; the population average hides it.
Nothing — aggregate performance is what matters.
The model should be retrained on all customers again.

div.p: Segment performance is the relevant question when the intervention targets a segment.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: A vendor says the model "proves" the training reduced turnover. What is missing?

choice.div: A causal design — without a comparison group, the claim is association.
Nothing; a model that predicts turnover also proves cause.

div.p: Prediction and correlation do not establish that the training caused the change.

choiceresponse.p: Which questions are legitimate to ask of a prediction model? Select all that apply.

choice.div: What is the base rate in this population?
What are the costs of false positives and false negatives?
Does it perform on the segment we will act on?
What data was it trained on, and how old is it?
Can it explain exactly why each individual behaved as predicted?

div.p: Base rate, error costs, segment performance and provenance are all fair. Individual causal explanation is usually not available from a predictive model.
